pgrust

A Rust rewrite of Postgres.

Try pgrust in your browser →   |   Discord   |   Updates   |   Issues

> **New:** [Video of Michael's talk at PlanetScale on pgrust](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7L_nG3EBjck) — and the [slides](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_wDk4HPE9-MuiPBo_X-QdJUmFtVV0p8p/view). > > [How AI Changes the Economics of JIT Compilers](https://malisper.me/how-ai-changes-the-economics-of-jit-compilers/) > > **v0.4-beta is out:** [the release post](https://pgrust.com/blog/pgrust-v0-4-beta/) and [what's new](#whats-new-in-v04-beta). pgrust is a re-implementation of Postgres meant to show what Postgres would look like if it was built in 2026. It is wire compatible and even SQL dialect compatible with Postgres. Every line is Rust, written to match the behavior of the C implementation. Rust makes it easy to re-architect several core Postgres pieces. pgrust has: - Gravity, a new vectorized push-based, JIT compiled query engine - A thread based concurrency model - A query scheduler designed to keep any individual query from taking down your database - An automatic memory manager: one memory budget, sized from the machine, covers the buffer pool, the columnar caches and running queries, and gives pgrust control of what happens when you're running low on memory, greatly reducing the chance of your whole DB being taken down by the OS OOM killer and many other really awesome pieces. The scheduler and the memory manager go after two of [the four horsemen behind thousands of Postgres outages](https://malisper.me/the-four-horsemen-behind-thousands-of-postgres-outages/). ## Quickstart **In your browser:** , a full pgrust server compiled to WebAssembly, no install. **On your machine:** download a release tarball from . Each one is self-contained: it carries pgrust's own `bin/postgres`, `bin/initdb` and `bin/psql` plus the share files they read, so you do not need a PostgreSQL install. The Linux binaries need glibc 2.34 or newer (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04, RHEL/Rocky 9 and later); the macOS binaries need macOS 11 or newer. | Tarball | Runs on | |---|---| | [`pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`](https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-x86_64.tar.gz) | any x86-64 CPU | | [`pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-aarch64.tar.gz`](https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-aarch64.tar.gz) | any 64-bit Arm CPU | | [`pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-x86_64-znver3.tar.gz`](https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-x86_64-znver3.tar.gz) | tuned for AMD Zen 3 and newer | | [`pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-aarch64-neoverse-v2.tar.gz`](https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-aarch64-neoverse-v2.tar.gz) | tuned for Neoverse-V2 (AWS Graviton4, NVIDIA Grace) | | [`pgrust-0.4-beta-macos-arm64.tar.gz`](https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-macos-arm64.tar.gz) | macOS on Apple Silicon | | [`pgrust-0.4-beta-macos-x86_64.tar.gz`](https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-macos-x86_64.tar.gz) | macOS on Intel | | [`pgrust-0.4-beta-macos-universal.tar.gz`](https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-macos-universal.tar.gz) | macOS, either (both architectures in one binary) | The Linux builds are profile-guided optimized. The tuned builds use instructions only those CPUs (and newer ones) have; when in doubt, take the generic build. Every tarball has a `.sha256` file next to it, and [`MANIFEST.txt`](https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/MANIFEST.txt) lists them all. ### Linux ```bash # Pick your build: linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64, linux-x86_64-znver3 or # linux-aarch64-neoverse-v2 (see the table above). PLATFORM=linux-x86_64 # Download pgrust, verify the checksum and unpack it. curl -LO "https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz" curl -LO "https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256" sha256sum -c "pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256" tar xzf "pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz" cd pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-*/ # Create a data directory with pgrust's initdb. bin/initdb -D /tmp/pgrust-data --no-locale --encoding UTF8 -U postgres # Start the server. It runs in the foreground and logs to this terminal. ulimit -s 65520 RUST_MIN_STACK=33554432 bin/postgres \ -D /tmp/pgrust-data \ -k /tmp -p 5432 \ -c listen_addresses= \ -c io_method=sync \ -c max_stack_depth=60000 ``` Leave the server running and connect from a second terminal, in the same directory: ```bash bin/psql -h /tmp -p 5432 -U postgres -c "select version()" ``` You should see `PostgreSQL 18.6 (pgrust 0.4-beta, build ) on ...`, where `` is the short commit the binary was built from. `bin/postgres --version` prints `pgrust 0.4-beta (PostgreSQL 18.6 compatible)`. ### Docker The prebuilt image on Docker Hub, [`malisper/pgrust`](https://hub.docker.com/r/malisper/pgrust), is a drop-in replacement for the official `postgres` image: same env vars (`POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, `POSTGRES_USER`, `POSTGRES_DB`, `PGDATA`, ...), same `/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d` init scripts, same data volume at `/var/lib/postgresql/data`. It carries the same `postgres` and `initdb` binaries as the Linux release tarballs above, and initializes the cluster with pgrust's own `initdb`; the only C PostgreSQL component in the image is `psql` for the init scripts. `malisper/pgrust:v0.4-beta` is multi-arch (amd64 + arm64); `v0.4-beta-amd64` and `v0.4-beta-arm64` pin one architecture. ```bash docker run -d --name pgrust -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -p 5432:5432 malisper/pgrust:v0.4-beta ``` Then connect, with your own `psql` or the one in the image: ```bash psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U postgres docker exec -it pgrust psql -U postgres ``` `malisper/pgrust:latest` still points at v0.3; use the `v0.4-beta` tag to get this release. A data volume written by v0.3 holding columnar tables needs the dump and restore described under [Stopping, restarting, cleaning up](#stopping-restarting-cleaning-up). ### macOS ```bash # Pick your build: macos-arm64 (Apple Silicon), macos-x86_64 (Intel) or # macos-universal (both). PLATFORM=macos-arm64 # Download pgrust, verify the checksum and unpack it. Download with curl: curl # does not set the quarantine flag a browser download gets, so Gatekeeper stays # out of the way (see the note below). curl -LO "https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz" curl -LO "https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256" shasum -a 256 -c "pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256" tar xzf "pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz" cd "pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM" # Create a data directory with pgrust's initdb. bin/initdb -D /tmp/pgrust-data --no-locale --encoding UTF8 -U postgres # Start the server. It runs in the foreground and logs to this terminal. ulimit -s 65520 RUST_MIN_STACK=33554432 bin/postgres \ -D /tmp/pgrust-data \ -k /tmp -p 5432 \ -c listen_addresses= \ -c io_method=sync \ -c max_stack_depth=60000 ``` Leave the server running and connect from a second terminal, in the same directory: ```bash bin/psql -h /tmp -p 5432 -U postgres -c "select version()" ``` **A note on Gatekeeper:** the macOS binaries are signed ad hoc, not notarized by Apple. Downloaded with curl as above, they are never quarantined and none of this comes up. If you download with a browser instead, macOS refuses to run them with "Apple could not verify ... is free of malware". Clear the flag with `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM`, or approve each binary under System Settings > Privacy & Security > "Open Anyway". ### Columnar tables Columnar storage (`pgrcolumnar`) is a table access method. Register it once in each database, then create tables with `USING pgrcolumnar`: ```sql CREATE ACCESS METHOD pgrcolumnar TYPE TABLE HANDLER heap_tableam_handler; CREATE TABLE events (id bigint, kind text, val double precision, at timestamp) USING pgrcolumnar; ``` ### Stopping, restarting, cleaning up - **Stop the server** with Ctrl-C in its terminal, or `kill -INT `. That is Postgres' fast shutdown and it is safe. - **Start it again** by rerunning the same server command with the same data directory. Your data is preserved across restarts. - **Start over** by deleting the data directory: `rm -rf /tmp/pgrust-data`. This deletes all data in it. - **If startup fails with** `FATAL: lock file "/tmp/.s.PGSQL.5432.lock" already exists`, another server, most likely an existing Postgres install, is already using port 5432. Start pgrust on a different port with `-p 5433` and connect with `psql -h /tmp -p 5433 -U postgres`. Whenever a regular Postgres is running on the same machine, check `select version()` after connecting; it is easy to silently connect to the wrong server and wonder why nothing behaves like pgrust. - **If startup fails with** `could not open directory "/usr/local/pgsql/share/timezone"`, the server cannot find its share files. It reads them from the `share` directory beside the binary, so run `bin/postgres` from the unpacked tarball as is, without moving the binary away from `bin/share`. `PGRUST_PGSHAREDIR` and `PGRUST_TZDIR` point it elsewhere. - **Columnar tables from v0.3** (`USING pgrcolumnar`) are refused with an error saying the table is in the v0.3.x columnar format. Dump them with the v0.3 binary (`pg_dump`) and restore them into v0.4-beta. ## Status We don't recommend running pgrust in production (yet), but we are successfully running it ourselves internally. pgrust

A Rust rewrite of Postgres.

Try pgrust in your browser →   |   Discord   |   Updates   |   Issues

New: Video of Michael's talk at PlanetScale on pgrust — and the slides.

How AI Changes the Economics of JIT Compilers

v0.4-beta is out: the release post and what's new.

pgrust is a re-implementation of Postgres meant to show what Postgres would look like if it was built in 2026. It is wire compatible and even SQL dialect compatible with Postgres.

Every line is Rust, written to match the behavior of the C implementation. Rust makes it easy to re-architect several core Postgres pieces. pgrust has:

  • Gravity, a new vectorized push-based, JIT compiled query engine
  • A thread based concurrency model
  • A query scheduler designed to keep any individual query from taking down your database
  • An automatic memory manager: one memory budget, sized from the machine, covers the buffer pool, the columnar caches and running queries, and gives pgrust control of what happens when you're running low on memory, greatly reducing the chance of your whole DB being taken down by the OS OOM killer

and many other really awesome pieces. The scheduler and the memory manager go after two of the four horsemen behind thousands of Postgres outages.

Quickstart

In your browser: https://pgrust.com, a full pgrust server compiled to WebAssembly, no install.

On your machine: download a release tarball from https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/. Each one is self-contained: it carries pgrust's own bin/postgres, bin/initdb and bin/psql plus the share files they read, so you do not need a PostgreSQL install. The Linux binaries need glibc 2.34 or newer (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04, RHEL/Rocky 9 and later); the macOS binaries need macOS 11 or newer.

Tarball Runs on
pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-x86_64.tar.gz any x86-64 CPU
pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-aarch64.tar.gz any 64-bit Arm CPU
pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-x86_64-znver3.tar.gz tuned for AMD Zen 3 and newer
pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-aarch64-neoverse-v2.tar.gz tuned for Neoverse-V2 (AWS Graviton4, NVIDIA Grace)
pgrust-0.4-beta-macos-arm64.tar.gz macOS on Apple Silicon
pgrust-0.4-beta-macos-x86_64.tar.gz macOS on Intel
pgrust-0.4-beta-macos-universal.tar.gz macOS, either (both architectures in one binary)

The Linux builds are profile-guided optimized. The tuned builds use instructions only those CPUs (and newer ones) have; when in doubt, take the generic build. Every tarball has a .sha256 file next to it, and MANIFEST.txt lists them all.

Linux

# Pick your build: linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64, linux-x86_64-znver3 or
# linux-aarch64-neoverse-v2 (see the table above).
PLATFORM=linux-x86_64

# Download pgrust, verify the checksum and unpack it.
curl -LO "https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz"
curl -LO "https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256"
sha256sum -c "pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256"
tar xzf "pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz"
cd pgrust-0.4-beta-linux-*/

# Create a data directory with pgrust's initdb.
bin/initdb -D /tmp/pgrust-data --no-locale --encoding UTF8 -U postgres

# Start the server. It runs in the foreground and logs to this terminal.
ulimit -s 65520
RUST_MIN_STACK=33554432 bin/postgres \
  -D /tmp/pgrust-data \
  -k /tmp -p 5432 \
  -c listen_addresses= \
  -c io_method=sync \
  -c max_stack_depth=60000

Leave the server running and connect from a second terminal, in the same directory:

bin/psql -h /tmp -p 5432 -U postgres -c "select version()"

You should see PostgreSQL 18.6 (pgrust 0.4-beta, build <commit>) on ..., where <commit> is the short commit the binary was built from. bin/postgres --version prints pgrust 0.4-beta (PostgreSQL 18.6 compatible).

Docker

The prebuilt image on Docker Hub, malisper/pgrust, is a drop-in replacement for the official postgres image: same env vars (POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_DB, PGDATA, ...), same /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d init scripts, same data volume at /var/lib/postgresql/data. It carries the same postgres and initdb binaries as the Linux release tarballs above, and initializes the cluster with pgrust's own initdb; the only C PostgreSQL component in the image is psql for the init scripts. malisper/pgrust:v0.4-beta is multi-arch (amd64 + arm64); v0.4-beta-amd64 and v0.4-beta-arm64 pin one architecture.

docker run -d --name pgrust -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -p 5432:5432 malisper/pgrust:v0.4-beta

Then connect, with your own psql or the one in the image:

psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U postgres
docker exec -it pgrust psql -U postgres

malisper/pgrust:latest still points at v0.3; use the v0.4-beta tag to get this release. A data volume written by v0.3 holding columnar tables needs the dump and restore described under Stopping, restarting, cleaning up.

macOS

# Pick your build: macos-arm64 (Apple Silicon), macos-x86_64 (Intel) or
# macos-universal (both).
PLATFORM=macos-arm64

# Download pgrust, verify the checksum and unpack it. Download with curl: curl
# does not set the quarantine flag a browser download gets, so Gatekeeper stays
# out of the way (see the note below).
curl -LO "https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz"
curl -LO "https://pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-beta/pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256"
shasum -a 256 -c "pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256"
tar xzf "pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM.tar.gz"
cd "pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM"

# Create a data directory with pgrust's initdb.
bin/initdb -D /tmp/pgrust-data --no-locale --encoding UTF8 -U postgres

# Start the server. It runs in the foreground and logs to this terminal.
ulimit -s 65520
RUST_MIN_STACK=33554432 bin/postgres \
  -D /tmp/pgrust-data \
  -k /tmp -p 5432 \
  -c listen_addresses= \
  -c io_method=sync \
  -c max_stack_depth=60000

Leave the server running and connect from a second terminal, in the same directory:

bin/psql -h /tmp -p 5432 -U postgres -c "select version()"

A note on Gatekeeper: the macOS binaries are signed ad hoc, not notarized by Apple. Downloaded with curl as above, they are never quarantined and none of this comes up. If you download with a browser instead, macOS refuses to run them with "Apple could not verify ... is free of malware". Clear the flag with xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine pgrust-0.4-beta-$PLATFORM, or approve each binary under System Settings > Privacy & Security > "Open Anyway".

Columnar tables

Columnar storage (pgrcolumnar) is a table access method. Register it once in each database, then create tables with USING pgrcolumnar:

CREATE ACCESS METHOD pgrcolumnar TYPE TABLE HANDLER heap_tableam_handler;

CREATE TABLE events (id bigint, kind text, val double precision, at timestamp)
  USING pgrcolumnar;

Stopping, restarting, cleaning up

  • Stop the server with Ctrl-C in its terminal, or kill -INT <pid>. That is Postgres' fast shutdown and it is safe.
  • Start it again by rerunning the same server command with the same data directory. Your data is preserved across restarts.
  • Start over by deleting the data directory: rm -rf /tmp/pgrust-data. This deletes all data in it.
  • If startup fails with FATAL: lock file "/tmp/.s.PGSQL.5432.lock" already exists, another server, most likely an existing Postgres install, is already using port 5432. Start pgrust on a different port with -p 5433 and connect with psql -h /tmp -p 5433 -U postgres. Whenever a regular Postgres is running on the same machine, check select version() after connecting; it is easy to silently connect to the wrong server and wonder why nothing behaves like pgrust.
  • If startup fails with could not open directory "/usr/local/pgsql/share/timezone", the server cannot find its share files. It reads them from the share directory beside the binary, so run bin/postgres from the unpacked tarball as is, without moving the binary away from bin/share. PGRUST_PGSHAREDIR and PGRUST_TZDIR point it elsewhere.
  • Columnar tables from v0.3 (USING pgrcolumnar) are refused with an error saying the table is in the v0.3.x columnar format. Dump them with the v0.3 binary (pg_dump) and restore them into v0.4-beta.

Status

We don't recommend running pgrust in production (yet), but we are successfully running it ourselves internally. Keep Postgres as the source of truth for data you can't afford to lose.

pgrust still has a lot of bugs. Our #1 priority right now is testing and reliability.

If you need production ready Postgres today, use Postgres.

PostgreSQL extensions don't work out of the box: there is no stable extension ABI in pgrust yet. But pgrust ships a large number of them, including pgvector, pg_cron, pg_stat_statements, pg_trgm, hstore, pgcrypto, postgres_fdw and most of contrib. PL/Python, PL/Perl and PL/Tcl are not supported yet.

Performance

Measured on c8g.4xlarge (AWS Graviton4), pgrust with pgrcolumnar, its builtin columnar layout, runs ClickBench's analytical queries up to 1,600x faster than PostgreSQL (per query, cold runs, against PostgreSQL's published results on the same instance type).

For a code-level walkthrough of one part of that speedup, read how batching, operator fusion, and SIMD speed up the query engine.

Writing

  • How AI Changes the Economics of JIT Compilers: building a copy-and-patch ARM64 JIT in Rust.
  • pgrust: Rebuilding Postgres in Rust with AI: why we started the project.

Testing

The most common question we get about pgrust is: how can anyone trust it? Passing a test suite doesn't mean our code is correct. Getting to the point where people can trust pgrust is our number one priority today.

To achieve that goal, we're taking several different approaches:

  1. Of the 3,400 user facing Postgres functions, we've formally verified that 1,397 have identical behavior in pgrust with Kani; 466 more are tested against Postgres. The ledger is proofs/USER_FACING_FUNCTIONS.tsv.
  2. We're engaging with Antithesis to do simulation testing of pgrust to battle test pgrust.
  3. We're doing aggressive differential fuzz testing to ensure pgrust's behavior is identical to Postgres's.

Unsafe Code

pgrust uses unsafe code, but only for the specific things that need it. Postgres represents every internal value as a Datum, an untyped 8 byte value, and Rust has no safe equivalent, so the code that packs and unpacks internal values is unsafe. The same goes for the places where pgrust must match Postgres' memory layouts byte for byte.

If there are particular unsafes that are not necessary and removing them would not have an impact on performance, let us know, as we would love to remove more unsafes.

Building from source

You need the Rust toolchain (any rustup install works; rust-toolchain.toml pins the build to Rust 1.96.0 and rustup fetches it automatically) and the RE2 regex library:

  • Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt-get install -y build-essential pkg-config libre2-dev
  • macOS: brew install re2 pkg-config
cargo build --release --locked -p main_main -p initdb

select version() names the build: a build in a git checkout prints its short commit (PostgreSQL 18.6 (pgrust 0.4-beta, build 1a2b3c4) on ...); set PGRUST_BUILD_ID at build time to choose the id, or build outside git for none. postgres --version prints pgrust 0.4-beta (PostgreSQL 18.6 compatible); postgres -V prints postgres (PostgreSQL) 18.6, the line PostgreSQL's own pg_ctl, initdb and pg_upgrade check.

The server binary lands at target/release/postgres, pgrust's initdb beside it, and the share tree it needs (postgres.bki, the setup SQL, timezone, timezonesets, tsearch data, extension files) is staged at target/release/share/. No C PostgreSQL is involved in creating or running a cluster:

target/release/initdb -D /tmp/pgrust-data --no-locale --encoding UTF8 -U postgres
ulimit -s 65520
RUST_MIN_STACK=33554432 target/release/postgres -D /tmp/pgrust-data \
  -k /tmp -p 5432 -c listen_addresses= -c io_method=sync -c max_stack_depth=60000

The time zone database is PostgreSQL 18.6's own compiled tzdata, read from share/timezone beside the binary (never the host zoneinfo, like C built without --with-system-tzdata). To use the system zoneinfo instead, build with PGRUST_SYSTEM_TZDATA=/usr/share/zoneinfo (C's --with-system-tzdata); PGRUST_TZDIR and PGRUST_PGSHAREDIR remain runtime overrides, not requirements. A data directory made by stock PostgreSQL 18 initdb still works too (same on-disk format). Release builds refuse to compile without RE2 on purpose: a build with only the fallback regex engine is drastically slower on regex heavy workloads. The binaries we publish additionally use --profile dist, which turns on fat LTO; it produces a faster binary but takes much longer to compile.

What's new in v0.4-beta

  • Gravity, a new query engine. Gravity runs every query and every kind of statement (DML with ON CONFLICT and RETURNING, triggers, row locks, cursors, PL/pgSQL and SPI, COPY) with PostgreSQL's semantics, on columnar tables and on the ordinary row store alike. It replaces our previous engine and runs analytical queries as much as 3x faster than ClickHouse. Its JIT was rewritten around a new low-level IR: it compiles each plan to AArch64 or x86-64 machine code, and to WebAssembly in the browser build, or interprets it when compiling would not pay off.
  • pgrcolumnar grows up. pgrcolumnar stores compressed, immutable parts with zone maps, delete vectors and background compaction. Reads see PostgreSQL MVCC snapshots, and writes are transactional: they roll back with the transaction. Small inserts land in a row-store front that is folded into columnar parts in the background, and UPDATE and DELETE mark rows in delete vectors instead of rewriting parts (ON CONFLICT and MERGE are not supported on columnar tables yet). Columnar tables take non-unique B-tree, hash, GiST, SP-GiST and GIN indexes, are written to WAL, so they survive crashes and replicate to standbys, and support row locks and a sorted_by table option.
  • One memory budget covers the buffer pool, the columnar caches and running queries. Near the memory limit pgrust cancels the statement holding the most memory instead of letting the OS kill the server.
  • jsonb statistics. ANALYZE collects statistics on the keys and values inside jsonb columns, and the planner uses them for ->, ->>, #>, #>> and ?, ?|, ?&, so it estimates jsonb filters instead of guessing. On by default (pgrust.jsonb_path_stats).
  • The condition cache. Filter results on columnar tables are reused across statements over the same immutable data. full is the default (also spelled on) and stores match counts too. rows keeps row selections and per-dictionary-code filter tables without counts; granule keeps only empty-granule verdicts; off disables predicate reuse. pgrust.dict_filter_cache and pgrust.zone_store turn off the per-dictionary-code filter tables and the zone-map result store on their own. Sizing feedback, data caches, and startup prewarm have separate controls.
  • pgrust's own initdb, and pg_cron 1.6 is included.
  • Upgrading: columnar tables from v0.3 must be dumped and restored. UTF8 is the only server encoding.

v0.4-beta is a beta: it shows what is coming in v0.4 while we finish stabilizing the rest.

Developing in the open

Up to v0.3 we developed pgrust privately and published it in large monthly releases. Starting with v0.4-beta, development happens in this repository: features, optimizations and bug fixes are pushed here as soon as they are ready, instead of being held back for the next release.

Implementation

Executor

  • Gravity, a vectorized, push-based executor that compiles plans to machine code (AArch64 and x86-64) with a JIT that emits code directly.

Parallelism

  • Threads instead of processes, for both connections and parallel query.
  • A query scheduler, new to Postgres. Queries get a priority, and long-running queries have theirs lowered, so heavy queries interfere less with fast ones.
  • Parallel query rebuilt around work stealing: idle threads are assigned dynamically to speed up queries already in flight.

Storage

  • pgrcolumnar, a column-oriented format with dictionary encoding and several other compression schemes, WAL-logged.
  • Pipelined fsync. A worker releases its locks after calling fsync but before it completes. This is safe because the query is not acknowledged, and none of its effects are observable, until the fsync finishes.

Other

  • The automatic memory manager. Near the machine's memory limit, pgrust cancels the statement holding the most memory, so that one query dies and the server itself can keep running.

Roadmap

Next we're working on testing and battle testing pgrust and making it so people can trust pgrust with their data.

Beyond that we want to add:

  • Instant forking
  • Autoscaling including scale to zero
  • Planner support for JSON
  • Undo log support for a no-vacuum design
  • Adaptive planner to prevent bad plans
  • A mini version of pgrust designed for testing and being embedded

Contributing

We are not actively accepting pull requests right now. If you want to help out with the project, reach out on Discord.

Please do still open an issue if something breaks, if setup is confusing, or if there is a Postgres behavior you want matched.

releases.name: pgrust v0.4-beta
releases.body:
pgrust v0.4-beta is a beta: it shows what is coming in v0.4 while we finish stabilizing the rest. Read the release post: https://pgrust.com/blog/pgrust-v0-4-beta/

## What's new

- **Gravity, a new query engine.** Gravity runs every query and every kind of statement (DML with ON CONFLICT and RETURNING, triggers, row locks, cursors, PL/pgSQL and SPI, COPY) with PostgreSQL's semantics, on columnar tables and on the ordinary row store alike. It replaces our previous engine and runs analytical queries as much as 3x faster than ClickHouse. Its JIT compiles each plan to AArch64 or x86-64 machine code, and to WebAssembly in the browser build.
- **pgrcolumnar grows up.** MVCC snapshots, transactional writes, a row-store front for small inserts, UPDATE and DELETE through delete vectors, background compaction, WAL logging (crash safety and replication), non-unique B-tree, hash, GiST, SP-GiST and GIN indexes, row locks, and a `sorted_by` table option.
- **Automatic memory management.** One memory budget covers the buffer pool, the columnar caches and running queries. Near the memory limit pgrust cancels the statement holding the most memory instead of letting the OS kill the server.

releases.name: v0.3.1
releases.body:
# pgrust v0.3.1

v0.3.1 is a bug-fix release on top of v0.3, still compatible with Postgres 18.6.

## Fixes

- Fix whole-row record references while preserving fields literally named `"*"`.
- Fix duplicated COPY notice context.
- Decode only the requested prefix for LZ4-compressed TOAST slices.
- Fix BRIN indexes with custom operator classes to use their own support functions instead of the built-in ones.
- Fix integer percentile ordering and transaction statistics accounting.

## Upgrade

Rebuild existing BRIN indexes that use custom operator classes with `REINDEX`.

pgrust is still experimental and not for production.

releases.name: v0.3: Try us on real world workloads in non-critical environments
releases.body:
Releasing pgrust v0.3, our Postgres rewrite from C to Rust. This release is mostly about making pgrust more reliable. Try it on real world workloads in non-critical environments.

pgrust is not production ready. Do not put data you care about in it. If it behaves differently from Postgres, please [open an issue](https://github.com/malisper/pgrust/issues) with a reproduction.

## What's new in v0.3

- We're now on PostgreSQL 18.6, including its bug and security fixes.
- `cbstore` is now `pgrcolumnar`. Update SQL that uses `USING cbstore` to `USING pgrcolumnar`; the old name no longer works.
- `version()` now reads `PostgreSQL 18.6 (pgrust 0.3)`.

See the [README](https://github.com/malisper/pgrust/blob/main/README.md) for setup, and the [full commit history](https://github.com/malisper/pgrust/commits/v0.3) behind this release.

releases.name: pgrust v0.2: Now faster than Postgres and Clickhouse
releases.body:
Releasing pgrust v0.2. This is the fast version of pgrust, our Postgres rewrite from C to Rust. pgrust v0.2 is faster than Postgres and Clickhouse.

## Performance

Measured on `c8g.4xlarge` (AWS Graviton4) against PostgreSQL 18.3.

On the ClickBench combined score, pgrust scored 18.5% faster than ClickHouse
and hundreds of times faster than PostgreSQL. This was using pgrcolumnar,
pgrust's builtin columnar layout.

On sysbench-oltp, pgrust achieved 30% higher throughput than Postgres 18.3 on
read-only workloads at 300GB scale.

These runs were reviewed independently by **Greg Smith**, author of
*PostgreSQL 9.0 High Performance*.

Two honest caveats. We had previously reported that pgrust was over 50%
faster than Postgres. On Kubernetes we measure a larger OLTP gap, 50-60%
rather than 30%, and we have not isolated why the same binaries behave
differently there than on bare EC2, so we quote the lower number. Second, the
binaries we publish are generic for their architecture. The benchmark numbers
come from builds tuned for Graviton4 (`-Ctarget-cpu=neoverse-v2`), so you
will not reproduce them exactly from a download.

aiSummary.oneLiner: A high-performance Rust reimplementation of PostgreSQL 18 designed to be 300x faster for analytics.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: pgrust is an ambitious ground-up rewrite of PostgreSQL 18.3 in Rust, prioritizing execution speed and demonstrating what Postgres would look like if built today. It achieves full wire and SQL dialect compatibility, passing all 46,066 official Postgres regression tests to ensure strict behavioral parity with the original C implementation. The project leverages Rust's safety to introduce a new vectorized push-based JIT compiled executor, a thread-based concurrency model, and a custom query scheduler. These architectural changes allow it to outperform both standard Postgres and ClickHouse on specific analytics benchmarks when tuned for Graviton4 processors.
keyFeatures: Strict regression parity: Validates absolute correctness by passing 100% of the 46,066 tests in the official PostgreSQL 18.3 regression suite.
Vectorized JIT executor: Replaces the traditional Postgres executor with a new vectorized, push-based, JIT compiled engine tuned for Graviton4.
Thread-based concurrency: Uses a modern thread-based concurrency model to vastly improve throughput compared to standard Postgres process forks.
Built-in OOM killer: Includes a custom Out-Of-Memory killer that provides graceful degradation rather than allowing the OS to kill the entire database.
Formal verification: Utilizes Kani to formally verify that over 1,000 user-facing functions have identical behavior to the original C implementation.
